Senses.Explanation: On a battlefield, 'defeat' (敗) is a rout and 'breach' (闕) is a gap. In Chinese Chan records the compound is a recurrent verdict of failure on an exchange, statement, answer, or speaker. The allowlisted corpus has 594 hits in 193 texts. It records the constructions 'incur a failure' (納敗闕, 130 hits in 80 texts), 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕, 129 hits in 85 texts), and 'the place of the failure' (敗闕處, 39 hits in 28 texts). In one direct exchange a monk asks, 'What failure do I have?' and receives the answer 'Wrong.' Elsewhere Dahui quotes Linji calling an old man's response 'a failure today,' then answers the question 'Where is his failure?' with 'The road is far and the night is long; stop carrying a torch, everyone, and blow it out while walking in the dark.' Yuan Cheng is asked how to have no failure and replies, 'Eat three meals.' A later comment can apply the verdict to both parties while also calling both adept: 'As failures, both are failures; as adepts, both are adepts.' These records leave the verdict attached to the cited exchange rather than supplying one universal defect that the word always names.
Senses.Note: The word carries a military register: 'rout' (敗) plus 'breach' (闕) becomes a verdict that an exchange has failed, as in 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕) and 'incur a failure' (納敗闕). All seven required definition formulas were searched; none produced a lexical definition. The entry therefore foregrounds the direct 'what failure?' exchange, the 'where is the failure?' retrospective, verdict uses, and the corpus's own two-party contrast. The rare 'no failure' construction (無敗闕) has one hit in one text. Exact actors are named on every retained occurrence except the source-anonymous questioning monk, whose reviewed exception record preserves all six attribution rungs.
